title: Due process and judicial compensation
primary_topics: CJ due process objection to Gamboa v. Teves: foreign investors whose property rights would be adversely affected were never summoned or given the opportunity to be heard

The history and complexity of the adjusted judicial compensation framework under RA 9227 (SAJ), subsequent Arroyo salary increases, and the Joint Resolution No. 4 tranches -- and the new SC resolution of June 7, 2011 attempting to stabilize judges pay
sub_topics: Gamboa v. Teves (June 28, 2011, J. Carpio): foreign investments in public utilities limited to 40% of voting shares; SEC has uniformly held since 1935 that entire capital stock is used in determining 40% allocation -- foreigners invested relying on this representation

Due process objection: foreigners most adversely affected were never summoned or heard; one foreigner mentioned in title not served with petition; Pangilinan sued as managing director of First Pacific but First Pacific itself not included; foreign chambers of commerce not impleaded

Constitution Bill of Rights: No person shall be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law -- person includes foreigners and corporations forced to unload investments at bargain prices
Themistocles: Strike, but hear me first! Webster: due process is a law that hears before it condemns, proceeds upon inquiry, and renders judgment only after trial
CJ refrains from discussing substance; confines comment to absolute need for due process without which any decision would be void

Judicial compensation history: RA 9227 (effective Nov. 11, 2006) doubled compensation via Special Allowance for Justices and Judges (SAJ) -- implemented during CJ tenure; filled ~600 vacancies (30% of trial courts); decent pay to discourage graft

After CJ retired: GMA twice increased basic pay by 10% each time -- increases for judges charged to SAJ; increases formed part of basic salaries and subjected to withholding taxes (unlike non-taxable SAJ) -- take-home pay effectively decreased despite nominal increases
Joint Resolution No. 4 (June 17, 2009): revised Salary Standardization Law; four yearly tranches starting 2009 -- again charged to magistrates SAJ
New SC resolution (June 7, 2011): pay tax-free retroactively from June 24, 2010; SAJ as of Nov. 11, 2006 preserved; base pay increases taken from SAJ; DBM covers deficiency if SAJ insufficient
New problems: SAJ insufficient to cover full pay increases -- rank and file cease getting SAJ surpluses; SC may be forced to increase docket fees (chagrin of poor litigants)
CJ recommendation: Congress should fund pay increases from national coffers, as done for other government offices -- not rely on SAJ

stances.claim: Gamboa v. Teves is procedurally void regardless of whether its substantive ruling is correct, because foreign investors whose property rights would be adversely affected were never summoned, served, or given the opportunity to be heard -- no court, not even the Supreme Court, may impose obligations without first hearing those most adversely affected.
stances.rhetorical_move: due-process-void argument as the overriding procedural objection

stances.claim: The post-RA 9227 trajectory of judicial compensation is a cautionary tale: GMA 10% increases and Joint Resolution No. 4 tranches were both charged to the SAJ, effectively decreasing judges take-home pay rather than increasing it (increases became part of taxable base pay while SAJ was non-taxable).
stances.rhetorical_move: good-intentions-bad-outcomes diagnosis of the judicial compensation history

stances.claim: Congress should fund judicial pay increases from national coffers -- as done for all other government offices -- rather than forcing the SC to increase docket fees, which would burden poor litigants.
stances.rhetorical_move: congressional-funding-recommendation to relieve the SAJ deficit

notable_anecdotes: Themistocles Strike, but hear me first! and Daniel Webster law that hears before it condemns -- CJ two canonical due process anchors deployed against the Supreme Court own failure to hear affected foreign investors.

The paradox of the judicial pay trajectory: GMA 10% pay increases actually decreased judges take-home pay -- because increases were charged to the non-taxable SAJ and reclassified as taxable basic salary.
The docket-fee-burden-on-poor-litigants risk: if the SAJ is insufficient, the SC may be forced to raise filing fees -- directly burdening the least resourced litigants.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban raises a fundamental due process objection to Gamboa v. Teves (June 28, 2011, J. Carpio): the foreign investors whose property would be adversely affected -- forced to unload investments at bargain prices -- were never summoned or given the opportunity to be heard. The SEC had uniformly construed 'capital' as including all shares since 1935; foreigners invested relying on this representation. Yet the decision does not show they were summoned; one foreigner mentioned in the title was not served; First Pacific itself was not impleaded; and foreign chambers of commerce were not joined. The Constitution (Art. III Sec. 1) protects 'persons' including foreigners and corporations -- invoking Themistocles ('Strike, but hear me first!') and Daniel Webster ('a law that hears before it condemns'). CJ refrains from discussing the substance and confines his comment to the absolute need for due process, without which any decision would be void. In the second part, CJ traces the torturous judicial compensation history: RA 9227 (effective Nov. 11, 2006, implemented during his tenure) doubled judicial pay via the tax-free SAJ, filling 600 vacancies. But GMA's subsequent 10% pay increases and Joint Resolution No. 4 tranches were both charged to the SAJ and reclassified as taxable basic salary -- effectively decreasing judges' take-home pay despite nominal increases. The new SC resolution (June 7, 2011) attempts to stabilize the framework retroactively from June 24, 2010, but new problems arise: the SAJ may be insufficient, forcing the SC to raise docket fees -- burdening poor litigants. CJ recommends Congress fund judicial pay increases from national coffers, as done for all other government offices.
